title: Expressions, Types, and Value Categories
relevance: Interviewers use value categories to check whether candidates can explain assignment legality, where expressions may appear, and why pre- and post-increment differ.

phases.goal: Establish what an expression produces and that every expression has both a type and a value category.

must_hit.point: Every expression has two properties: a type and a value category.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States both properties and that they together decide how an expression may be evaluated and where it may appear.

must_hit.point: An expression is evaluated to produce a result, may have side effects, and can evaluate to objects or to functions.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions result, side effects (e.g. ++x persists after evaluation), and that expressions can yield objects or functions.

must_hit.point: An lvalue evaluates to an identifiable object—something with a name and a fixed location that can be referred to again later; rvalues are not lvalues and evaluate to a value.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts identifiable named objects (lvalues) with non-identifiable values that must be used immediately (rvalues).

must_hit.point: Lvalues are either modifiable or non-modifiable; non-modifiable lvalues cannot have their value changed because the object is const or constexpr.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives both subtypes and ties non-modifiable to const or constexpr objects.

probes: What two properties does every C++ expression have, and what does each one tell you?
What is the difference between an lvalue and an rvalue?

hints.1: Think beyond the value the expression computes—C++ tags every expression with another property that controls where it may appear.
hints.2: Name the two properties, then define lvalue versus rvalue in terms of identifiable objects versus bare values.
hints.3: Every expression has a type and a value category; an lvalue is an identifiable object (modifiable or const/constexpr non-modifiable), and an rvalue is not an lvalue and evaluates to a value.

phases.goal: Explain assignment operand rules and lvalue-to-rvalue conversion.

must_hit.point: The assignment operator requires its left operand to be a modifiable lvalue expression and its right operand to be an rvalue expression.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States both sides of the rule and uses it to explain why x = 5 is valid and 5 = x is not.

must_hit.point: lvalue-to-rvalue conversion: when an rvalue is expected but an lvalue is supplied, the lvalue is evaluated to produce its value.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains why x = y compiles: y is an lvalue that converts to its value for the right-hand side.

must_hit.point: Unless stated otherwise, operators expect their operands to be rvalues; arithmetic on lvalues works because the lvalue is read for its value.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Notes the default operand expectation (e.g. operator+) and that lvalues are usable there via their values.

probes: Why is x = 5 legal but 5 = x illegal when both sides are int?
If assignment expects an rvalue on the right, how does x = y compile when y is an lvalue?

hints.1: Type alone does not decide assignment legality—look at what each side’s value category must be.
hints.2: State the left/right assignment requirements, then name the conversion that lets an lvalue appear where an rvalue is expected.
hints.3: Left must be a modifiable lvalue and right an rvalue; for x = y, y undergoes lvalue-to-rvalue conversion so its value is assigned.

phases.goal: Establish the conversion asymmetry that is the heart of the value-category model.

must_hit.point: An lvalue will implicitly convert to an rvalue, so an lvalue can be used anywhere an rvalue is expected.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says named objects can stand in wherever a value is needed because they are read for their value.

must_hit.point: An rvalue will not implicitly convert to an lvalue, so a bare value cannot stand in where an addressable, named object is required.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the one-way nature of the conversion and that this asymmetry is central to the model.

probes: Can an lvalue be used where an rvalue is expected? Can an rvalue be used where an lvalue is expected?
Why does the language allow reading a named object as a value but not treating a bare value as a named object?

hints.1: Ask which direction of conversion is implicit and which is not.
hints.2: Frame it as asymmetry: values versus addressable named objects.
hints.3: Lvalues convert to rvalues implicitly; rvalues do not convert to lvalues—so a named object can supply a value, but a bare value cannot act as an addressable object.

phases.goal: Classify common expressions by value category, including string literals and the increment operators.

must_hit.point: A named variable is an lvalue; a temporary like std::string("Hello") constructed on the fly is an rvalue.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Classifies the named variable as identifiable/lvalue and the unnamed temporary std::string as rvalue.

must_hit.point: A C-style string literal such as "Hello" is an lvalue because it is stored as an array of characters in a read-only section of the program’s memory and has a permanent memory address.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Calls out the quirk versus numeric literals and ties lvalue status to permanent address/storage.

must_hit.point: Pre-increment ++x is an lvalue because it returns the actual modified variable x; post-increment x++ is an rvalue because it returns a temporary copy of the old value.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts returning the modified variable itself versus returning a temporary copy of the old value.

probes: Is "Hello" an lvalue or an rvalue, and why might that surprise someone?
What is the value category of ++x versus x++, and why do they differ?

hints.1: Do not assume every literal is an rvalue—string literals are a special case.
hints.2: For increments, ask what each operator actually returns: the variable itself or a copy of the old value.
hints.3: "Hello" is an lvalue (read-only character array with a permanent address); ++x returns the modified variable (lvalue); x++ returns a temporary copy of the old value (rvalue).

tradeoffs.strong_answer: An lvalue implicitly converts to an rvalue, so a named object can be used wherever a value is needed; an rvalue will not implicitly convert to an lvalue, so a bare value cannot stand in where an addressable, named object is required.

++x adds to x and returns the actual modified variable x, so the result is an lvalue; x++ must return the old value after updating x, so C++ creates a temporary copy of the old value and that temporary is an rvalue.

tradeoffs.topic: numeric literals vs C-style string literals
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Numeric literals such as 5 are rvalues; C-style string literals are lvalues because they are stored as arrays of characters in read-only program memory and have a permanent memory address.

gotchas.trap: Using type alone to explain why x = 5 is valid but 5 = x is not.
gotchas.correction: Both can be int; assignment requires a modifiable lvalue on the left and an rvalue on the right, so 5 = x fails because 5 is an rvalue.

gotchas.trap: Treating C-style string literals like numeric literals as rvalues.
gotchas.correction: "Hello" is an lvalue: it is stored as a character array in read-only memory and has a permanent address.

gotchas.trap: Assuming ++x and x++ have the same value category.
gotchas.correction: ++x returns the modified variable itself (lvalue); x++ returns a temporary copy of the old value (rvalue).

gotchas.trap: Thinking x = y should fail because y is an lvalue where an rvalue is expected.
gotchas.correction: y undergoes lvalue-to-rvalue conversion, which evaluates y to produce its value for the assignment.
